MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: Order. If the house would subside perhaps the Chair could hear the hon. member.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext:
I was rising on a question of privilege, which I am seeking to do in a thoroughly non-contentious way, with respect to a return made to a question which I asked and which was made an order for return on October 22, and to which the return was furnished yesterday. I draw Your Honour's attention to one part of the question only and to the return made thereto by the Department of Veterans Affairs. The question was:
Has a benevolent fund been set up for exprisoners of war captured at Hong Kong from the war claims fund as recommended by the veterans affairs committee of the House of Commons and. if not, why not?
The answer to that was "No". Now, I recognize that if this had been a question answered in the house I would have no right under the rules to have made any complaint about it, but this was made an order for return. It then became an order of the house; therefore there was an obligation on the department and the minister to make a full reply as the house ordered it to be made, and the failure to do so of course is, in a technical sense, in contempt of the house.
I am not seeking to make this point except in a purely technical way. I am quite sure neither the minister nor the department intended any such thing, but it is an important matter and the privileges of hon. members and of the house are involved.
I am not just drawing attention to this particular return. I venture also to draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that it is very important, if questions are to be made orders for returns, that very careful consideration should be given to the terms of these questions so the returns can be made in accordance with the orders.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: What government sent Canadian soldiers to Hong Kong?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: Great Britain asked for them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: Order. The point the hon. member raised really has some relation to the question as to whether on an oral question or an ordinary written question it is open to an hon. member to comment on the sufficiency or insufficiency of the answer Here again I think we could have perhaps 260-odd versions of what might be sufficient for the hon. member's question in so far as an answer is concerned. It must also be considered that the minister and the department involved must take the question as they find it on the order paper. Some questions, the hon. member will agree, are well drafted; others are somewhat less well drafted. Therefore I do not know that a question of privilege arises in relation to the quantum or the sufficiency of the answer. I think there might be a point-and I am subject to correction here-if the answer were to mislead or were to be incorrect; then perhaps, if it is within the knowledge of the hon. member who has asked the question that the answer is obviously wrong, he might have something to say. But as to the sufficiency of an answer, I am highly doubtful as to whether there is a true question of privilege.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext:
If Your Honour will hear me on the point of order Your Honour has raised, I would agree completely with Your Honour if this were an answer to a question. But the point I am making is that it is not an answer to a question. This is a return in compliance with an order of the house, an order made at the instance of a minister of the crown. If the minister of the crown was not satisfied with the wording he should not have asked the house to make an order in those terms. That is the whole point. He should have answered it, in whatever fashion he wished, in the house. But once an order of the house is made by the whole house, then it becomes an order of the house. It is a well recognized principle that the government, being responsible to the house, and the ministers individually being responsible for their departments, once an order of the house has been made-as it was in this case-that order must be complied with.
That was the whole of my point. I am not arguing for one minute that I or any other hon. member has a right to complain about an answer, whether it is an answer on the orders

Question of Privilege
of the day or an answer given in response to a question on the order paper. Your Honour is absolutely right about that. It is for the government to take whatever responsibility it likes, and we cannot complain about those answers. But this is an order of the house, made by this house at the request of the minister. The question is very simple. It is "If not, why not?", and the answer to that, sir, cannot possibly be no.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: That may be, in this particular instance, but I hesitate to think that the hon. member would be setting up a double standard for answers; that a lesser degree of care might be exercised in replying to ordinary written questions, or starred questions, and there should be a greater degree of care given to those which are made orders for returns. If there is any suggestion of that in the hon. member's representations to the Chair, I do not think the Chair could for one moment entertain that sort of double standard. I think there is one standard that applies all the way through, and I think the hon. member would recognize that.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could be heard further on the point. The very point here is that the standard that applies to questions is not applicable to an order of the house. Once an order of the house issues a minister has no choice in the matter; he must either comply with that order or move to have it discharged. There are certain procedures for doing that. The point at issue here is as to whether or not there is compliance with the order of the house. The order having been issued, then the minister no longer has that discretion in relation to the answer he may give to a question; he has no such discretion left to him. It is an order of the house and he must comply with it, unless he takes certain other remedies that are set out in the rules, having to do with a motion to discharge the order.
The point is of such importance that I am wondering if I could, with respect and propriety, ask Your Honour if you would consider reserving the question and dealing with it at a later time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: I think perhaps we might do that, although I would once again reiterate that I do not think there should be any question of a double standard. Unfortunately that, to me, at the moment is implicit in some of the remarks which have been made. However, I will accede to the suggestion made by the hon. member and I will take the matter under advisement.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: May I say just a word on this point?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  ANSWER TO QUESTION MADE ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext: The Chair has decided to take the matter under advisement, and I think we will pass on to something else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement with respect to the participation of the federal government in Canada's bid for the 1968 winter Olympic games.
As the house knows, an engineering survey financed by my department recommended that a proposal involving the use of the Banff-Lake Louise area would provide this country with the strongest hope of selection as host for this international event. I now wish to advise that my colleague, the Minister

of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and I intend to allocate additional funds to further this project, as a firm indication that the bid has the support of the federal government.
It has been decided that my department will bear the responsibility of federal aspects of matters relating to the operation of the games and for provision of the necessary funds to cover all federal grants and subsidies. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources will deal with all matters relating to developments within Banff national park, and will provide necessary funds to cover all federal capital expenditures in this area.
To date $139,000 has been spent federally on this project. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources will spend a further $35,000 this year toward providing capital construction needed to bring this site up to Olympic standards. If surplus funds are available, an additional $25,000 will be allocated to secure cost analyses by suitable consultants.
Further funds will be sought through the estimates of the next fiscal year so that the Calgary Olympic development association will be given the utmost federal support in its application to the international Olympic committee a year from now. If our bid is successful it is anticipated that total federal costs involved in staging the games will be in the neighbourhood of $8 million. It is my hope that parliament will see fit to grant further funds year by year to meet our commitments.
It has been most heartening to observe the support this project has been given by the public and all levels of government. My department's $35,000 operational grant to C.O.D.A. was matched by the province of Alberta and the city of Calgary, and these matching arrangements will, I expect, be maintained. Efforts at the local level deserve the highest praise, and I think much of the credit must go to C.O.D.A.'s president, Mr. Ed. Davis, and to the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith).

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S VOTE ON RESOLUTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Would the minister inform the house what instructions have been given to the Canadian delegation as to how Canada should vote tomorrow on two resolutions regarding a nuclear test ban, which are before the political and security committee of the United Nations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NUCLEAR TESTING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S VOTE ON RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been two resolutions before the first committee, one brought in by the eight non-aligned countries and co-sponsored by 25 or 26 others and another resolution brought in by the United States and the United Kingdom.
Yesterday Canada introduced amendments to the first resolution to which I have referred. In so doing we had several aims. One was to insert in the resolution a reference to the letters which had passed over the week end between President Kennedy, Premier Khrushchev and Prime Minister Macmillan. Then in the operative part of the resolution we are seeking to add a paragraph which urges that if there should not be agreement right away between the nuclear powers on all types of testing, at least there should be agreement with regard to tests in the atmosphere, under water and in outer space. This Canadian amendment was just tabled yesterday afternoon and is under debate today. I therefore do not know as yet what the result will be.
On Monday when I was in New York we circulated another resolution. We had hoped to get it agreed unanimously, but that was not possible. The Soviet union refused to accept this resolution. We are now hoping, of course, that our amendments to the eight nation resolution will be accepted. There probably will not be a vote until tomorrow.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-71, to amend the Farm Credit Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. C-71 is to amend the Farm Credit Act of 1959, to provide for an increase in the Farm Credit Corporation's capital from $12 million to $16 million, to eliminate some anomalies and restrictions which experience has demonstrated to be unnecessary to the successful operation of the act, to provide for greater flexibility in the purposes for which farmers may borrow money from the corporation, and to broaden the role of the corporation in co-operation with ARDA in the vital field of agricultural readjustment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: Order. I wonder if hon. members would conduct their conferences outside the chamber so that the minister could be heard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
It will be recalled, Mr. Speaker, that the Farm Credit Act of 1959 had the effect of broadening the basis and increasing the amount of long term mortgage loans to Canadian farmers. The expressed objective of the act was:
To assist Canadian farmers in the voluntary reorganization of their industry into economic family farm units, each of which will be of sufficient size to produce, under the operation of the owner, the farm income necessary to meet all operating and maintenance costs, provide an adequate livelihood for the owner-operator and his dependants, and retire any required credit, with interest, within an appropriate term.
Canadian farmers quickly recognized the opportunities afforded them by this act. A
Farm Credit Act
total of 17,549 farmers have borrowed $198,804,900, an average of over $11,000 per loan, since the inception of the act for the express purpose of expanding and reorganizing their farms into economic family farm units.
Administratively, the Farm Credit Corporation has worked tirelessly toward the attainment of its objective. A survey shows that a large number of farmers have received loans in excess of the amounts applied for because, after discussion with the corporation's credit adviser, they realized they needed the additional credit to properly organize their farms. This surely is a positive indication that the corporation is going all out in its efforts to provide the necessary long term credit for the establishment of Canadian farmers on farm units of economic proportions. At the same time the regulations prevent loans from going to those who do not need them.
During debate on the resolution some hon. members of the official opposition were loud in their criticism of the objectives of the Farm Credit Act. They asked that we delete
economic units" and "adequate livelihood" from our objective and substitute "more economic units" and "more adequate livelihood". Apparently they do not believe that farmers should have an economic unit or an adequate standard of living, that something a little better than they now have will suffice. This government will settle for nothing less than adequate incomes for farmers. Anything less will merely perpetuate uneconomic units, delay inevitable adjustment and restrict the farm family to an inadequate living standard. It is an attempt by some of the official opposition to turn Canadians back to a peasant type of farming.
What happens to a Canadian farmer whose income is inadequate? I will tell you what happens. He does one or all of three things: (1) he lowers his standard of living, (2) he defaults on his mortgage or fails to pay his operating costs, (3) in his determination to maintain living standards and repay his credit obligations he exploits his soil resources, neglects maintenance and repairs, and makes no allowance for depreciation in buildings, equipment or livestock.
This surely is not the type of agriculture that we want. This is the type of agriculture that is bred in part by inadequate credit institutions with objectives that are less than they should be.
At this point I wish once again to draw the attention of the house to the chart taken from page 10 of the Farm Credit Corporation's annual report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1962. This chart vividly illustrates

Farm Credit Act
the niggardly assistance provided farmers by the previous administration, and with equal clarity illustrates the progressive advances this government has made in the matter of providing the credit essential for agricultural reorganization.
The success of farm credit, however, is not measured solely in terms of money. Associated with each application is an intensive program of pre-loan counselling, launched by the corporation. Broadly speaking the objectives of this counselling service are threefold; first, to ensure that the basic ingredients of productive land, adequate livestock, essential buildings and equipment are present in such amounts and quality as are normally essential for successful farm operation; second, that these essential ingredients are tied together in a practical plan of operation which, in combination with the farmer's operating and management skills, can be expected to produce sufficient income to cover the normal requirements of the farm business and provide the farmer and his family with an adequate standard of living. The third objective of the pre-loan counselling program is to influence the flow of investment capital into the various agricultural enterprises with the view of matching production to changing market requirements.
Hon. members will be interested to know that this is in fact being done. A recent analysis of the corporation's lending to dairy farmers reveals that a relatively insignificant part of the total credit granted to dairy farmers contributes directly to expanded production. On the contrary, the bulk of the credit has been provided for reorganization purposes within the industry. Concurrent with this, the corporation has recently been encouraging farmers who can profitably do so to convert from dairy to beef production. Thus our farm credit program is not only making contributions to the development of economically sound individual farm units, but is also making a significant contribution to the vitally important problem of matching agricultural production to market requirements.
Before moving on to other matters of importance, Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment briefly on the supervision program for part III farmers under the act. Eight hundred and twenty loans have been made under this section, the bulk of them in 1961 and 1962. Loans under part III have been somewhat slower than anticipated, and you will be asked to approve amendments to this section which your government believes will make part III substantially more attractive to prospective young borrowers.
You will also be asked to remove other restrictions which experience has shown to

be unnecessary and unduly restrictive. I do not believe that a valid assessment of the success of part III can be made at this time. Most borrowers have had their loans less than two years, and progress can hardly be assessed in that short period. It is perhaps significant to note, however, that such payments as have fallen due under this part have been promptly met, and the government sees advantages in further exploiting the potential of the supervised credit program.
The house will be further interested to know that the Farm Credit Corporation is presently working on the development of a system of electronic farm accounting. This system will not only reduce supervision costs, but more important it will serve to make possible the analyses of large numbers of farm records, returning to farmers concerned better information on the optimum use of their farm resources, and providing the corporation as well as federal and provincial research agencies with basic research material for such things as regional production costs. If this program can be developed successfully, the system of electronic farm accounting can move basic research in agricultural production economics, as well as farm management extension, to a new and higher level of achievement. Once again this government is demonstrating its ability to provide progressive leadership in the agricultural field.
May I at this point, Mr. Speaker, make reference to the Agricultural Stabilization Act of 1958 and to the Crop Insurance Act of 1959, introduced by this government. These two measures are playing a major role in reducing the risks arising from wide price and productivity fluctuations which hitherto have plagued Canadian agriculture and have been responsible for most of the extreme fluctuations in farm income. These measures, in contributing to the stability of agricultural income, have also created confidence in the field of agricultural credit. The risk hazard to the farmer and the lending agency has been reduced and the farmer, confident of his ability to repay, does not hesitate to ask for the credit he needs to establish a successful farm business.
Activities under the Farm Improvement Loans Act as amended in 1959 and 1961 are a further important consideration in the government's over-all credit program. When speaking on the resolution on Friday, October 26, I covered this subject in detail, and do not propose to repeat that information at this time. I would like to emphasize, however, that this type of credit is designed primarily to serve the intermediate credit needs of Canadian farmers, and in so doing it complements the services of the Farm Credit Act

and serves a very useful and significant role as part of the government's over-all program of farm credit.
I would like now to refer to the history of long term federal farm credit. The Canadian farm loan board was established in 1929, but its lending record was notably unenterprising until 1957, when this government took office. In the first 30 years of operation the farm loan board lent $183,160,586. The Farm Credit Corporation, in only three years of operation, has lent more than this, having approved a total of $198,804,900 from its inception on October 5, 1959 until September 30 of this year.
Here, Mr. Speaker, are the figures, both provincially and nationally, to show this comparison. What I am going to give now is a statement by provinces of farm loans approved to September 30, 1962. I will first of all give the province, then the figure for the amount lent under the Canadian farm loan board from 1929 until October 4, 1959, which is 30 years. Then I will give the amount lent by the Farm Credit Corporation from October 5, 1959 to September 30, 1962, which is three years: British Columbia, $8,751,181.97; for the last three years, $10,503,400; Alberta, $28,146,771.47 for 30 years as compared with $50,663,900 in three years; then Saskatchewan, $48,327,820.78 as compared with $57,028,900 in three years; Manitoba, $19,884,809.95 in 30 years as compared with $12,584,000 in three years; Ontario, $43,295,717.01 in 30 years as compared with $54,421,200 in three years; Quebec, $22,454,665.74 in 30 years as compared with $7,902,450 in three years; the Atlantic provinces, $12,335,619.19 in 30 years as compared with $5,701,050 in three years. Yes. The total for the country in 30 years was $183,160,586.11, and for the three years of the Farm Credit Corporation the figure is $198,804,900. From the foregoing discussion the house will begin to appreciate the comprehensive and progressive nature of this government's agricultural program, and something of the
Farm Credit Act
corporation's efforts in the field of agricultural reorganization. It also shows how we ended the tight money policy of the previous administration.
I am certain, however, that many hon. members must have in mind other groups of farmers who because of the physical nature of their land, or due to the lack of personal assets, or for a variety of other reasons, are unable to achieve the objectives of an economic farm unit on a solely agricultural basis. In keeping with this government's stated objectives in the field of agricultural readjustment, we believe the time has come to further exploit the success of farm credit legislation by extending it to include assistance to that large group of farmers who do not have the resources to be self-sustaining agriculturally, but who can obtain a reasonable standard of living by secondary off-farm income, or by virtue of their ability to develop and successfully exploit other non-agricultural pursuits on their farms. Part of the proposed amendments to the Farm Credit Act, as well as amendments to the regulations already approved by the governor in council, are devoted to this purpose.
I now wish to summarize the proposed amendments to the act for the convenience of hon. members.
The present authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation is $12 million, which permits the corporation to borrow $300 million from the Minister of Finance. The present total outstanding investment is $227,048,262.05. Because of the tremendous increase in volume of lending, the remaining funds will all be committed to borrowers by about next June. An amendment to the act will increase the capital by $4 million, providing an additional $100 million for the corporation to lend to Canadian farmers. If this is used, I will be back to ask for more.
To allow farmers greater flexibility in the use of the money they borrow, amendments are proposed which will permit the corporation to lend funds:
(a)	to make improvements to any part of the land the farmer is operating, including land, such as that on long term lease, which is not covered by the mortgage to the corporation;
(b)	to pay the farmer's operating and living costs during the first year or two, while he is developing his farm to the point at which it will produce the income necessary to meet these costs;
(c)	to help the farmer develop non-agricultural enterprises on his farm, such as camping grounds, tourist cabins, etc., if he can make more profitable use of his land resources in this way.

Farm Credit Act
Other amendments are proposed to eliminate some anomalies and restrictions which seem unnecessary.
Although the corporation has been making life insurance available to all borrowers, there is some doubt about its authority to do so for farmers who borrow under part II of the act. This authority is spelled out in the amendments.
Presently, if a farmer puts up land for security and joins in the mortgage to provide a loan to set up one son, he limits his eligibility for a loan in his own right, or to assist another son. One amendment removes this restriction.
At present a supervised loan must be fully disbursed before the borrower reaches his 45th birthday. It is proposed to amend the act to permit such a loan, provided it is approved by the corporation before the applicant has reached his 45th birthday.
So that the appraisal fee which a farmer must pay for a loan under part III of the act may be kept commensurate with that under part II, it is proposed to have it set by regulation, as it is for part II, rather than being prescribed in the act.
Supervised loans may now be made only to individual borrowers. An amendment proposes to make a farmer and his wife eligible as joint tenants. Couples frequently hold title to their property as joint tenants, and under the existing provisions of the act it is not possible to make a part III loan unless title is transferred to the name of the husband only. This seems to be an unnecessary interference with the manner in which a borrower may hold title to his property.
The amendments will also permit farmers who borrow under part III of the act to forgo supervision of their farming operations, if they so desire, when their debt has been reduced to 75 per cent of the value of their farm, rather than 65 per cent as at present.
Farmers who obtain supervised loans from the corporation are presently ineligible for loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act until their debt is reduced to 65 per cent of the value of their land or $20,000, whichever is the lesser. This sometimes forces them to seek credit elsewhere at high rates of interest. An amendment to the Farm Credit Act will make them eligible for farm improvement loans when their debt has been reduced to 75 per cent of the value of their land, and before that time at the discretion of the corporation.
Concurrent with the amendments we are proposing to the Farm Credit Act, amendments have been made to the farm credit regulations.

I cannot give the hon. member an answer offhand, but I think it was about two weeks ago, just at the time I introduced the bill. I had hoped to bring them out simultaneously, but I thought I would get this resolution and bill through a little faster than I have.
As I was saying, amendments have been made to the farm credit regulations. I wish to highlight these amendments and comment briefly on the effect they will have on the government's farm credit policy.
1.	A change in the basis of valuing farms will permit the corporation to attach greater importance to the value of farm buildings on specialized units. This will make it possible to lend to poultrymen, greenhouse operators, and other farmers who operate with costly buildings on relatively small areas of land.
2.	Another amendment will make eligible those farmers who must depend on other income for part of their living costs. In the past, only the income stemming from the production of the land could be considered in granting a loan. This restriction has been relaxed to take into account supplementary income from a number of sources. The corporation will now be able to recognize income from specialized operations based on the use of purchased feeds, as in the case of poultry and hog production; non-agricultural enterprises conducted on farms such as the operation of camping grounds or tourist cabins, etc., and revenue from outside sources, such as pensions, annuities or off-farm employment.
It will still be necessary, of course, that the applicant's principal occupation be farming. We do not intend that the Farm Credit Act be used to set up large commercial businesses; these are already adequately financed by the industrial development bank. This act was made for, and will continue to be used to assist, farmers who can show the corporation that with the use of credit they can increase their income and obtain a reasonable standard of living.
In conclusion, it is the contention of the government that the amended regulations, in conjunction with the amendments to the Farm Credit Act which the house is being asked to approve, will make a significant contribution to agricultural readjustment and stability. Many farmers, particularly in the older age groups, are unable to adjust to industrial pursuits but will, nevertheless, with the credit assistance proposed by this legislation, be able to achieve satisfactory standards of living and continue to retain their dignity and the respect of the community. At the same

time the legislation provides an opportunity for other farmers to develop non-agricultural pursuits for which their land, by virtue of physical characteristics or location, is particularly adapted.
The work of the Farm Credit Corporation up to this point has been in the organization of farm units which are economic solely from the agricultural point of view. It has gained experience and built up an efficient and enthusiastic organization. It is now ready to take on a broader task. The fundamental changes now being proposed will bring the corporation into close co-operation with the ARDA administration to form a team which will lead our assault upon the problems facing the small Canadian farmer.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture has just spoken on the second reading of this bill, and we now have the advantage of having the bill before us. When the minister spoke on the resolution stage I made the statement that he had used flowery language. Well, I was taken up on that statement and told that his language was not flowery. This bill and everything that goes along with it have been introduced with a great deal of fanfare, and on reading reports in the newspapers it appeared that it was really going to do something to make vast improvements in the administration of the Farm Credit Corporation. Some of these amendments which are before us, and some of the regulations of which the minister has spoken, are undoubtedly important and will be supported; but the bulk of them are very much of a technical nature and, while desirable and important, they are not very far reaching.
The minister has talked about the government's general attitude in regard to the kind of loans which are made. He went back to a fundamental definition which was put forward early in the discussion with regard to the administration of this act, and I thought we had moved him from this ground when I spoke first at the resolution stage and suggested that the definition should not be that of loans for an economic unit

in other words, if you have not got an economic unit you would not get a loan-but that it should be "loans for a more economic unit". The minister seemed to agree with that because on page 687 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
The hon. member was quite correct here. There should be a more economic farm unit-
Then he went on to say:
There were some new members who, probably in their innocence, told the committee that we have to give more loans to the small farmers. That is exactly what we have been doing. That makes the difference between what we have been doing for the last three years-

I suggest that while the minister has spoken about these amendments, there is very little in this legislation which will give the small farmer a chance. I should have liked to see something in this legislation, or in the changes in the regulations, which would make it clear-and it is not clear now-that in the administration of this act there would be a very substantial change from the situation which prevailed last year, when out of 14,517 documented interviews less than 6,000 applicants finally obtained loans. In other words, 55 per cent of the people who asked for loans and who had documented interviews were unable to get loans.
This is the contention of the members of the Liberal party; that there should be changes in the legislation itself, changes in the definitions by which it is administered, and changes in the regulations so as to place a much greater emphasis, a real emphasis, on the provision of more loans to the small farmers. Mr. Speaker, I say that the way this act has been administered recently shows that it is definitely weighted on the side of the larger farmers and larger loans.
The minister's very statements will support that contention. He goes on to talk about the aggregate sums of money lent, and everyone is in favour of that; but then he points out that the average size of loan is going away up. All that means is that, taking a certain aggregate sum of money, more emphasis is being given to larger loans. Of course the whole premise on which the administration of this act is based brings this about. The entire emphasis is on economic units instead, as we have suggested, of the loans being designed to bring about an improvement in the position of the farmers; and as long as that improvement is likely to take place, then they should be eligible for loans.

Farm Credit Act
The minister went on to talk about certain changes in the regulations. I am not going to tell the minister that they are not in effect; I am sure they must be. He has just told us that they are in effect. However, I have in my hand a copy of what was sent to me as purporting to be the changes in the regulations. No date is given on which changes were to have gone into effect. I am not arguing that they are not in effect; all I am saying is that what came out of the minister's office had no date on it.
However, I suggest that these changes are not adequate from our point of view. There will be the removal of a provision in the legislation which under part III requires certain appraisal fees. We have complained and protested most strongly against the $50 appraisal fee which was provided by regulation. This fee is away too high. It is a bar to the little farmer. It is an unjust tax on a farmer receiving a small loan-at least a farmer who got one-under this measure. It is another tax by order in council. Mr. Speaker, this sort of thing should be in legislative form. We cannot move an amendment at this stage to change this situation, though if there were a provision in the bill itself, we might be able to do so; but it is not in the bill; it is in the regulations. Unless the minister can stand up and tell me now that in these changes in the regulations the $50 fee will be reduced, I can only say to him that I am exceedingly sorry to see that there is no change in regard to this $50 fee in the regulations.

When he was speaking at the first stage of the resolution the minister said he was not doing too well in the maritime provinces, that not too many loans were being made. He wanted to see some improvement. Then when we all agreed that what he said was right and that the job was not being done in the maritime provinces, he makes another speech and says that if you relate the total amount of loans to the farm income in those provinces we have been doing about as well in the maritime provinces as we have been doing elsewhere. However, when he keeps contradicting himself in the various speeches he makes, it is extremely difficult to know just where he is going.
We had hopes that there would be a much greater indication in this legislation that something more would be done for the small farmers, that there would be greater emphasis on getting a greater number of loans to the marginal farmers, to the farmers who are having a difficult time, and that they would be loans of a size, even if they are small loans, that would help them improve their business. We thought there might be in this legislation some extra provision for loans for livestock. This has not been the case. The minister has put forward figures to demonstrate that loans are being made for this purpose under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, something of which we are all very much aware. However, I feel that under this legislation as well there could be a greater
Farm Credit Act
emphasis on the provision of loans for livestock. The governing consideration under this legislation is that all of the loans must have as security the farm land. This requirement makes it impossible to make many loans under this act for the extension of beef production.
The minister has an extremely difficult problem in the butter surplus in the country.
I think everybody agrees that any shift there may be out of butter production into the production of beef is something that should be supported. I had hoped that under this legislation, as was stated in the newspapers before it was introduced prior to the assembling of the house, there would be something to demonstrate that the government was endeavouring in a substantial way to encourage the increase of beef production. I see virtually nothing in this legislation designed in this direction. There are some amendments which will allow people who get loans under this legislation to get into other fields of activity, but there is nothing designed to bring about a substantial increase in the production of beef. We suggested earlier, and we do so again, that the best way in which to get improvements under this act is to have the whole thing aired before the agriculture committee of this house, and not brought before the committee after the legislation goes through. We do not think that procedure serves a very useful purpose. It may have some purpose. However, we do not think it serves a very useful purpose to say to the house, "Pass the legislation, make it the law, and then we will have a class of learners to hear what the officials of the Farm Credit Corporation have to say".

Mr. Speaker,
it is a pleasure to address the house once more to discuss the possibilities of farm credit in my riding, in the province of Quebec and in the whole of Canada.

When one studies this bill and listens to the remarks of the minister he wonders to what extent the minister's objectives and those of the various farm representatives differ. The Ontario Union Farmer of September describes the national farm union as being devoted to working toward the maintenance of the family farm structure in our agricultural policy. Canadian agricultural policies must be designed to supply stability and security for the average farm family so that they will enjoy a level of living comparable to that of other members of society.
References to a peasant society and upgrading the peasantry have been disturbing to some of us, because in a community like Leeds people have lived there for upwards of 200 years and they are not going to change, particularly in the matter of where they live or how they earn their living. We appreciate that there are problems and important shifts which must take place from time to time. I had hoped before the resumption of this debate to be able to refer to three statements

which the minister has made to the dairy farmers of Ontario and Quebec in which I think he gave warning that subsidies would be cut unless consumption dropped.
I think the hon. member made a mistake. He said the minister gave notice that subsidies would go unless consumption dropped. I do not think the minister said that.

I thank the Minister of Public Works. Of course, I meant to say "unless production dropped". The fact is that currently and, we think for a short period only, there is a serious problem of overproduction in dairy products. I have before me a copy of the Ottawa Journal of last night, October 31, in which the Minister of Agriculture addresses himself to this problem. The report is headed: "Dairymen may resist beef plan". This is the plan whereby the Minister of Agriculture suggests that dairy farmers will have to switch to beef. I am disturbed about this, because when I look at the answer to question 382, as it appears on page 1017 of Hansard, I notice, for instance, that fluid milk consumption has dropped from 405.10 lbs. in 1956 to 385.27 lbs. in 1961. This is serious. This really is the dilemma facing eastern Ontario. It is the fact, not that we have fewer people, although the population has not increased as much as we would have wished, but that the people we do have are drinking less and less milk. Again, the consumption of butter in 1956 was 20.51 lbs., and last year it was down to 16.43 lbs. We appreciate from the answer given recently to another question that the present volume of butter and butter oil is startingly high, but there is a great fear that the minister, who at times is decisive and makes long range plans which are sometimes implemented, may do something which could be very hurtful to the people in the community I represent, a community which has been established there for a long time.
I want to say to the minister that for many years the agricultural people in my type of area have tried to uplift themselves, preferably without loans from the Farm Credit Corporation, by doing exactly what they were advised, directed and guided to do, largely by the Ontario minister of agriculture, who told them that the way they were going to upgrade their production was to produce more, to have larger herds, to produce a better breed of cattle, and to raise breeding standards. Therefore, in a community such as Leeds, where the herds are chiefly Holstein, and some Jersey, there has been a
Farm Credit Act
great effort to improve herds, milk houses and coolers, and to go into large capital debt.
What has been the result of that? The result has been that the average income from our manufactured products is in the order, at the moment, of approximately $2.65 a hundred. You are wrong.

although everything seems to be all right at the Kingston level, the application does not go any further. These people do get discouraged, go to a member and ask the reason for this, and I suspect that the reason is a very real one.

While this is not always true, there is in the main a desire on the part of the corporation and their officials to see that the farmer can develop an economic unit. Much of the work in the initial interviews produces a result that would be satisfactory and then the application is applied for. In my area at least this is being done.

There is no question that there is some resentment on the part of individuals who feel that they should have received a loan. However, most of the resentment lies in the fact that their opinions of an economic unit and that of the advisory staff differ greatly, having regard to the manner in which an economic farm unit could be accomplished for the individual. In most of these cases no appraisal fee was paid because the matter was not pushed this far.
However, Mr. Speaker, this is not the main part of this bill. It is true that we needed more money but the main part of the bill is in that section which will allow the corporation the right to give assistance to the transfer from one type of economy in rural Canada to another type of economy and, while doing this, to supply the farmer with a livelihood and which will make this change operative if it is applied for. It should not be stated, as was stated by the hon. member who last spoke, that this legislation is going to be forced on the farmer. I would suggest that it is not going to be forced on the farmer by the government, but that it is going to be requested by the farmer himself. It is going to be forced on him by an economic situation over which neither the government nor the farmer has very much control.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH HOSPITAL SWEEPSTAKES BOARD
LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH HOSPITAL SWEEPSTAKES BOARD
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-16, to provide for the establishment of a hospital sweepstakes board.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of moving the second reading of Bill No. C-16 to provide for the establishment of a hospital sweepstakes board. If this measure passes, of course the board will be empowered to operate a national lottery. The object of the bill, as set out in the explanatory note and simply expressed, is to provide a legal outlet under strictly supervised conditions for those Canadians who wish to participate in a sweepstake or lottery on a national scale, and at the same time redirect or rechannel the proceeds from any such national lottery toward the promotion of the social welfare and public welfare of Canadians.
I know too, Mr. Speaker, that in introducing this bill I follow in the footsteps of a great many members of this house, both present and past, who have introduced similar legislation. I think we should be particularly indebted to a colleague of ours, the former member for Vancouver-Kingsway, Mr. Ferguson Browne. He, perhaps more than any other member, did a great deal of research and put considerable effort into bringing this matter to the attention of parliament during two sessions.
While this bill does set out in some detail the mechanics of how it is proposed a national lottery should operate, it is not my intention this evening to discuss anything more than the principle. In fact, it is my hope that we will deal with the principle because for too long we have argued about which charity or which welfare program the proceeds might be directed toward, and we have invariably found ourselves in some conflict about the principle in question. I submit, therefore, we must settle this issue first of all, and it is to this question that I turn my attention. I hope, in the next few minutes, to establish three points. The first is that today, as perhaps never before, there is a substantial demand,

I suggest an overwhelming demand, by the public for the establishment of a national lottery in Canada. I hope to reply, too, to some of those critics who, while constituting what I suggest is a small minority, have nevertheless registered objections which we in this house must acknowledge are sincerely held and with deep conviction.
In looking at the demand for a state lottery, one does not have to search very far through the daily reports in the newspapers to find one body or one group of individuals suggesting to this parliament that we amend the Criminal Code in order to make provision for a national lottery. Very briefly, it is interesting to note that two legislative assemblies, Quebec and Ontario, one by a vote in the house supporting a motion for a provincial lottery and in the instance of Quebec establishing legislation of a permissive nature, have supported this proposal. We are all familiar with the fact that municipalities in the various provinces, in particular Ontario and Alberta, recommended to their own legislative assemblies a lottery on a national scale, or at least a provincial lottery.
In so far as business and industrial support for this principle is concerned, recently the Canadian Chamber of Commerce offered a resolution in support of the principle to the executive committee at their annual meeting. The international railway brotherhood have offered their endorsation. The Canadian Trades and Labour Congress, through the officers of the international longshoremen and warehousemen union, have also offered their support to this principle.
What about the individual? We know that a short time ago a Gallup poll was taken in Canada, in 1956 to be exact, and it showed that 82 per cent of the people polled indicated their support of a national lottery. Then, more recently, I believe early in 1961 a survey was undertaken by La Presse, that well known publication, in the province of Quebec and the result of that poll was 98,780 in favour and 149 against. A group of women who belong to an organization known as "Operation Sweepstake" in my own city, developed a petition which I hope to present to parliament later this year. To date, they have obtained some 300,000 signatures in support of the principle of a national lottery. I personally pay particular tribute to one woman in this group, Mrs. Mamy English who went across this country, travelling some
12,000	miles, and at no time has she had anyone who in any way registered any objection to the principle of a national or state lottery. All of the major veterans organizations, the army, navy and air force veterans associations and the Canadian

Legion, have repeatedly at their annual meetings sent recommendations to parliament subscribing to this principle.
What is perhaps most interesting, sir, is the fact that this support does not come from any particular area or any particular classification of either age or economic status. In fact, my most recent group of petitions came from a number of old age pensioners in my own province. What is significant is that every area of Canada, every classification of people, have indicated for some years basic support of this principle.
Having established, I hope to the satisfaction of the house, that there is a demand, we might examine the objectives and principles of this type of legislation. What are we trying to accomplish? First of all, we realize that a substantial amount of capital goes out of Canada by the appeal of other national lotteries. There are some 70 of them, I believe, throughout the world. In fact, it is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, it is easier to select that state or country that does not have such a lottery than it is to identify those who are actually enjoying the benefits of such lotteries. Canadians have been participating in these lotteries of one type or another for a great many years. It is estimated, for example, that the Irish sweepstake, one of the better known, takes something like $10 million a year out of Canada. The total figure for all lotteries is probably closer to $100 million or $150 million a year. This, in itself, is not the most disturbing factor to me. I think it is going to follow that people will support lotteries probably under any circumstances.
What does bother me, sir, is the hypocrisy of the situation in Canada today in which the Criminal Code sets out certain regulations which govern lotteries within Canada, and those particular regulations are paid very little attention. There is no attempt to enforce them, and this is understandable. I am going to make certain references to a study that was made in 1956 by a committee of the two houses, the upper and lower houses of this parliament, and put before you one or two of their recommendations. I think before we make any assessment of the attitude of Canadians, we are pledged to pay some attention to what has been the experience with lotteries in other areas of the world.
The proceeds of Sweden's national lottery have benefited that nation in many ways, such as the provision of repertory theatres, sports facilities, scholarships, playing fields and so on and these, I believe, are testimonials to the value of the state lottery of that country.
The Swiss have been successful in assisting combat the major welfare problems of that country, and so have the Australians, the
Private Bills
Japanese, the Israelis, the Turks, the Spaniards, the Italians, the Portuguese, the French, the British and the West Germans. This therefore establishes beyond any doubt that we have throughout the world a great deal of experience to draw upon in guiding any legislation for a Canadian lottery. Yet in Canada, while we insist on accepting an archaic law to prevent even the most harmless games of chance, we close our eyes to the law as it stands, and as a consequence abuse of the present Criminal Code encourages lotteries to flourish on a private basis as never before in Canada.
In this respect I draw the attention of hon. members of the house to the report of the joint committee, some of the recommendations made in it, and comments on the evidence presented to it. The first of these appears in paragraph 8 of that report and reads as follows:
Lack of public support for lottery laws-The committee notes that there is widespread difficulty in enforcement and it is disposed to accept the statement of the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that there is a lack of support for the present prohibitory laws and that they cannot be enforced in the face of adverse public opinion.
Paragraph 9 says further:
The committee has little doubt that the results of this evasion of the lottery law are serious in that the law and law enforcement in general are thus brought into contempt.
Therefore we have a situation in Canada in which we are unable to enforce the present law of the state, and we will not recognize the advantages or opportunities that exist in a controlled or state lottery.
Many objections are raised by a great many people. I suggested earlier that we must examine these objections to examine what is the basis in fact, whether it is on a question of economics in the control of a lottery or its advantages, or whether it is purely on a moral issue.
On the basis of a moral issue it is my belief that this is a question for one's own conscience. If one considers it is immoral, or to use the words of one distinguished gentleman of the church that it will "corrupt the moral fibre of this country," might we not ask him if it has not the same effect on the peoples of Australia, New Zealand, Sweden and Switzerland? If we accept the principle that it would be immoral to hold a lottery in Canada, do we also subscribe to the principle that the provinces should not make profits on the sale of alcohol or impose taxation on horse racing?
I spoke to one of my colleagues a short time ago on this subject and he said that if it were not for the taxes raised on horse racing and the sale of alcohol in Ontario, they would not be able to pay for provincial educational costs. I do not know if that is true or not, but I do

Private Bills
make this point for these people inclined to criticize the principle of a state lottery on a purely moral basis: is there anything immoral in taking the proceeds from a state lottery and devoting them to the aid of people who are sick and people who need help, when it is a fact lotteries in one form or another already exist today in Canada.
There is a second objection raised, which to me seems more valid. That is the objection of whether or not a state lottery should be expected to maintain or sustain hospital construction, or perhaps any form of social welfare within a country. Basically I think this is one of the most misunderstood points in the whole argument. No one has ever suggested at any time that the proceeds of a state lottery should be the sole source of income for any particular charity or any particular social welfare. It would be ridiculous to assume that we could maintain hospital construction on the basis of the proceeds of any state lottery; but I can assure you, sir, those proceeds would be a very welcome source of income to assist in that important work.
There is a third objection which one hears from time to time. It is suggested that this is one of the most inefficient methods of raising money, but the facts do not bear that out. It is clearly indicated that in the instance of every major country in the world proceeds of lotteries have benefited those countries to a substantial degree.
I now wish to quote from the Toronto Star of March 6, 1961, which contained an article indicating that governments all over the world used the proceeds of lotteries to assist them in many ways. The article says:
Government around the world use the lure of lotteries-For up to 400 years governments have been supplementing their tax revenues through the earnings of officially sponsored lotteries-
It goes on to say:
Spaniards spend more than $50 million a year in their state-run lottery. Three drawings monthly decide the winners and the state takes 30 per cent. .. Ireland-the sweeps were established in 1930 to raise funds for hospitals. In the most recent one the gross reached $16 million,... so far the hospitals have received about $100 million while the government makes about $2 million a year.
Thus it is clearly established that a great deal of assistance could be given to the state by this very innocent form of gambling, and I hope I have established that we have a demand, such as never existed before, for a state lottery in Canada. There is a desire on the part of the individual to put money into a lottery of this nature, whether it be the Irish, the Spanish, the Mexican or a Canadian sweepstake, and the proceeds, in terms of aid to human beings could be measured by a more realistic yardstick.

When most community chests, united fund appeals and red feather agencies are out knocking on doors in an attempt to help a great number of agencies-and most of them have some difficulty-then surely this is the opportune time to give consideration to a national lottery of this kind?
To those who raise an objection of one type or another, I would only say that perhaps this debate is not the proper time to illustrate clearly the nature of their objection, whether it is a valid one or not, because I feel this bill will not be passed at this session; consequently it will go to the bottom of the order paper. However I would hope that the government, if nothing else, would agree to refer the bill to a joint committee of the two houses where people from every area could give evidence in support of it or raise objections to it. In such a committee we could constructively examine the advantages and disadvantages. We could study the types of aid which a sweepstake could provide in terms of social welfare and then, having heard the evidence, in the quiet calm of a committee room prepare a report upon which the house could later make an intelligent decision. I believe this is the only practical way, and I would ask the house to support that proposal if it cannot subscribe at this time to passing the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in supporting Bill C-16 submitted by my hon. fellow member from Calgary South (Mr. Smith).
The suggestion of forming a joint committee of both houses to study the matter is a timely one. As a matter of fact, people in general, and the members of the house, have discussed for many years whether it would be fitting to set up national lotteries for the benefit of hospitals and various charitable organizations.
Hon. members are certainly aware that, in the past, some of them have actively tried to make the public aware of the fact that such a bill would be a sensible one. I want to associate myself with my fellow members from Quebec and the other provinces who have actively promoted that idea and proclaimed the necessity of instituting in this country some sweepstakes or lotteries for charitable purposes.
I would also stress the interest shown by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), my former colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) and all other members of parliament, as well as the members of social groups concerned with the matter, and who will be gratified if the bill is accepted.
I also would like to point out, Mr. Speaker -I do not want to inject any partisan flavour into the discussion-that the Conservative party has for a long time been interested in this legislation, because, in 1951, at the national convention here in Ottawa, I had the privilege of submitting, as president, of the Quebec Young Conservatives, a similar resolution which was accepted by the majority of the Young Conservatives Association of Canada.
It may be said that the Conservative party, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) stated a moment ago, that is, that we were slow to evolve, had foreseen the need of such legislation more than ten years ago.

Private Bills
There is no doubt that today the people's views have evolved in this matter. My hon. fellow member from Calgary South mentioned the results of a public opinion poll which took place in the province of Quebec under the sponsorship of La Presse, and which clearly showed that more than 99,482 people were in favour of such a plan, whereas only 149 disapproved it. This proves that interest in this matter is increasing and that the idea is progressing among our population.
Mr. Speaker, I have also submitted a similar measure for the operation of provincial lotteries in order to financially assist hospitals and charitable institutions. If the provisions are somewhat different, the principle of the measure I have put on the order paper is the same.
After submitting my bill, I received several letters, particularly one from Vancouver. I wish to quote from that letter to show that from coast to coast, public opinion on lotteries and gambling did evolve.
(Text):
Georges Valade, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
Congratulations on submitting Bill No. 56 which I hope the house will pass.
I would like to submit for your consideration that the bill should provide that only those over 55 and the physically handicapped could be employed in lotteries.
And so on.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in reading a few extracts from this letter was simply to show the interest aroused throughout the country by such bills.
The house is no doubt aware also of the fact that more than 600 boards of trade, throughout the country, have conducted public opinion polls to that effect. The results clearly indicate that 70 per cent of the Canadian population want their representatives to put forward their views in the house on this matter and also to express their full support for this kind of legislation.
For the guidance of those sympathizing with certain groups who exert pressures and put forward objections which, to my way of thinking, are not very serious nor fully justified, I must explain that gambling is almost innate in human beings.
In fact, one has but to study the history of gambling itself to realize that games of chance are quite old. In 1562, for example, the bull in eligendis declared void the bets which were being made on the election of the pope. Around the year 27, the Romans drew

lots on the robe of a crucified man. Later, archeologists inquiring into the ruins of primitive societies unearthed bones, cut in cubes, and dotted like dice.
As can be seen, games of chance are human because they are universal and ancient. They show, first of all, a need for relaxation and amusement, and then, the need to get a lot for almost nothing.
Those who are opposed to games of chance place lotteries in the same category, and the main objection brought forward is that of morality or of immorality.
In fact, some conscientious objectors consider very immoral the fact that some people contribute a dollar to take the risk of getting cash profits, but they forget that the morality or the immorality of an act depends on the intention and on the conscience.
For their guidance, I should like to read what has been published in this regard in a report submitted by Mr. Leon Trepanier, in April 1936, on the question of lotteries. The following extract, to be found on page 11, is entitled "Conscientious objectors":
(Text):
"Conscientious objectors"
To legalize lotteries would be to violate Christian morals . .. teach the young to gamble ... a principle of "unsound economy".
And the stock exchange, whose unbridled speculations multiply suicides, ruin homes and turn thousands of young people into criminals; is the stock exchange a school of morals?
Allow a poor devil to buy legally a $1 lottery ticket, that is teaching him to gamble. But, on the other hand, the dominion parliament, by a law adopted in 1912, allows anyone to toss away his savings at races at Woodbine, Connaught Park, or Blue Bonnets. That is not encouraging gambling!
A principle of "unsound economy".
(Translation):
In my estimation, that is the answer to those who are conscientious objectors to lotteries because of principles they could not even define.
In my opinion, our gambling law is most ridiculous. In fact, according to section 254 of the Criminal Code, people travelling on trains are prohibited from playing cards for money. However, if these same players use discs, chips or some other gimmicks like matches, for instance, to pay for what they have lost at the game and later exchange them against the money they owe, everything becomes legal and those whose conscience is easily aroused are relieved.
Mr. Chairman, gambling is immoral if there is excess. If there is no excess, it is

permitted, because gambling may involve three things: intelligence, ability and chance.
But if it implies intelligence and ability, the less it is interesting unless there is added to it the incentive of a prize to gain. It is therefore a game of chance. And it is to the game of chance that is added the money risk.
Is that money risk immoral? That is the main question.
Is it more moral to risk $200 on a hunting trip and to come home with an empty bag, than to risk $1 on a lottery ticket for charitable purposes?
Are not two persons who draw lots on a restaurant bill engaged in a game of chance in which money is involved?
Therefore, if gambling in itself is legitimate, and if to risk money on a game of chance is per se authorized, how can we consider immoral that particular game of chance?
Those games of chance are not bad in themselves, as long as they keep within the bounds of morals, and avoid accidental elements which could make them immoral, such as cheating and exploitation, such as the risk of losing what does not belong to the gambler. In other words, a gambler may not risk the money he needs to ensure the welfare of his family, and he may not have as main motive the desire to win in itself, because he must prevent his gambling from becoming a passion. Those are elements which could have an immoral character.
But when lotteries, as the hon. member for Calgary South suggested, are designed to procure funds for charitable purposes, in order to help hospitals, they involve elements which, by themselves, stand apart from the immoral aspect of the matter.
I therefore suggest that such lotteries would be moral.
The purpose of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Calgary South therefore automatically eliminates all objectionable elements. So I suggest there is nothing immoral in the fact that Canada should finally decide to refer to a joint committee of both houses this matter of lotteries, in order that we may have the views of the members of the house on this matter.
Mr. Speaker, if you were to ask the hon. members of this house who are in favour of this project to raise their hand, I am sure that more than 90 per cent would be in favour of lotteries. Those who would be opposed to lotteries or who would abstain from voting would probably do so under the pressure of certain groups having definite views on the matter, or out of personal con-27507-3-76

viction, or else for political expediency, or again through lack of understanding of the meaning and scope of lotteries.
I would have liked to deal at greater length with the moral aspect of this matter, because I suggest that this is the main objection to this bill concerning lotteries.
The Catholic church is not against lotteries when they comply with moral standards. This bill has nothing whatsoever to do with religion; but we should not end up, after mentioning that point of view, by discussing the subject in the light of our religious beliefs.
I feel it would be advisable to restrict ourselves to the principle of the bill. But we should take into account the views of persons qualified to discuss the moral aspect of this resolution. The opinion of Cardinal Griffin on this matter is worth mentioning. This is what he said:
Let us keep in mind that it is the abuse and not the games of chance themselves that must be denounced and that certain puritan views on the subject should be corrected.
The English, the French, the Irish, the Australians, the Swiss and others who take part in lotteries to help their hospitals, would they be less moral than we are?
In spite of prohibitions, the Americans venture each year more than $20 billion in gambling, illicit or otherwise.
In Canada, are we exempt from gambling because of that legislation which restricts the authority of the provinces or the federal government in the field of lotteries? Does it give us a better protection against gambling which takes place behind the scenes and secretly at the prejudice of the honest citizens of this country?
I suggest that it would be more advisable for the government to amend the Criminal Code or legislate in this field to be able to stop abuse and control the disbursements made for lotteries.
If it is considered immoral to buy a lottery ticket for $1, I wonder what our morals mean, when the head of a family goes to the races and destroys not only his future but also the future of his children, all that under the protection of the law which permits racing bets.
As my colleague was saying a while ago, is there anybody in this house who has never bought a sweepstake ticket or taken part in the army and navy subscription in Canada? How many of us have not been taken in by those dishonest people who, under cover of the law, print counterfeit lottery tickets and sell them on the market, without even giving the purchaser, however well-intentioned he may be, a chance to win a prize for his money.

That is because the law, in making lotteries illegal, protects those who take advantage of credulous people and use the law to exploit honest citizens.
If we had lotteries, Mr. Speaker, we would keep in our country the hundreds of millions of dollars which, these last few years, are being sent to foreign countries often richer than we are. That money could be put to much better use by our hospitals and our welfare organizations.
In conclusion, I should like to quote from an editorial published in La Presse on January 30, 1962, dealing precisely with morality of lotteries, and signed by Marius Girard:
In the meantime, under the pretext of shielding the virtue of Canadians against temptations, we allow the Irish hospitals to take out of Canada millions of dollars, not to mention the incomes provided to organizers of illicit lotteries which, as we know, have a tendency to proliferate. But by allowing certain lotteries to be arranged under close control conditions, fondness for gambling could be used to the benefit of Canadian institutions, as it was provided for in the legislation voted by the Quebec legislature in 1934 and 1950.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only a few minutes. Being no expert on lotteries, I think I should be the last person to take part in this debate, but there are one or two things I should like to say in connection with this bill. First of all, I am aware that the question might arise in the minds of many people whether the government should be getting into the lottery business as such, or whether or not, if lotteries are to be made legal, other associations should operate them within the confines of the regulations set up by the government. In this case the government would not be precipitating lotteries by an act of parliament. I also think that if it ever comes to the point where we do have lotteries-and I do not doubt for one moment that the time will come when that is so, and it may not be too far off-no advertising of any kind should be allowed in order to pressurize or to get people to buy lottery tickets, or in any way induce people to do things. It should merely satisfy the gambling spirit which is inherent in the human being. I think that commissions or advertising should be completely out of the picture, because as hon. members know, individuals who cannot afford to buy a lottery ticket could under pressure be induced to buy one if a commission was offered or there was any advertising.
I think that if we are to get a clear picture of the thinking of people-and I have listened with great interest to the figures quoted this afternoon in connection with polls, plebiscites,

and that sort of thing-the joint committee which might study this question might see fit to find the means of putting the question before the people by way of a plebiscite along with a general election, so that everyone could, without pressure or undue advertising and publicity from pressure groups, and so on, decide for themselves and give a clear mandate to the government to move in a certain direction.
