subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house adjourned at five o'clock to consider other business I was mentioning that this particular act, and the amendments that are proposed, are revolutionary in character. I am surprised, after reading the press releases the minister issued, the articles in the Western Producer and other newspapers, to find no emphasis put upon the provision giving the corporation power to make loans when changes in the farmer's economic unit are indicated.

I believe this is a good change, a worthwhile change. I am surprised the minister has not made more of it, that more consideration has not been given to this particular section. I believe that this change is revolutionary enough to warrant sending the bill to the committee on agriculture and colonization. I believe we should have the opportunity of hearing the views of farm organizations on this particular change, as well as other persons who may be interested. In the last few days there has been some speculation in the Ottawa newspapers on this subject. Some questions were asked, according to yesterday's Journal, by various provincial officials as to whether or not there would be a change to beef production in the eastern part of Ontario. Some of the comments that were made were rather surprising and because these comments were made by certain people, I think this warrants an investigation to ascertain whether or not the proposed changes will be in the interests of the farmers concerned.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt at all but that these changes will be advantageous. I believe that farmers will gradually, must gradually, take advantage of this legislation. This provision will mean that the small dairy farmer who is shipping milk to the cheese factory or the creamery and who is getting a small cheque each month will be able to discuss with officials of the corporation whether or not it would be advantageous for him to change his whole program from a small dairy operation into a large beef producing unit. It might also mean that, along with the application of ARDA, a farmer could decide he wished to go into the Christmas tree business, poultry production, hog production or make some other change in his farm unit.
No doubt the criticism of this suggestion will be and must be, as the hon. member for Leeds pointed out, that the federal government and the corporation must not be in a position to tell the farmer he is to go out of dairy production in which he has been for many years, and go into beef production. I strongly suggest that some assurance should be given that loans will not be granted on the basis of a predominant beef production or the predominance of any segment of agriculture. These loans must be granted upon the same conditions as loans granted by the corporation in other categories. The basis must be the operation of a farm as an economic unit operated under the supervision of the corporation. I feel assurance must be given that the government will not use the credit corporation to make changes in our agriculture economy, and that the corporation will take the wishes of the people concerned into consideration.
27507-3-764
Farm Credit Act
I do not envisage these changes coming all at once. If all the farmers in eastern Ontario were to decide tomorrow that they wanted to take advantage of this section to go into beef production, there is no question in my mind as to what would happen to our agricultural program in so far as support prices for beef are concerned. However, I think this is not likely to happen. The officials of this corporation have the experience and the leadership of a person like Mr. Rutherford, who has concentrated on getting the farmer to accept and demand the amount of credit the advisory committee considers would be advantageous to him in the establishment of an economic unit. I do not believe this feature is going to change.
There will be, Mr. Speaker, farmers who will not want to take advantage of this particular section, even if it were good for them. There is no question but that there are farmers who will say: I have made a living, my father has made a living and my grandfather has made a living in the production of milk or cheese and I shall continue to do so. I do not believe the corporation should force a farmer to take advantage of this section against his wishes, because the individual farmer is still going to have to ask for the loan and is going to have to prove that an economic unit can be established.
No doubt there are other changes that will be mentioned. I am not so sure that we have not gone so far that the other fields of endeavour in which a farmer may engage may sooner or later distract him from the farm operation itself. It is and has been advantageous, however, for farmers to have a few cabins on their farms if they are located in areas where this is possible. Some of them have a small motel or garage operation. I am pleased that the minister is considering this as a supplementary source of income to the farm operation itself. I think this is an advantage and will be welcomed by the farmer.
I have always been of the opinion that it was almost impossible for a person to go into farming operations in Canada when he was not in a position to meet the requirements of this act. As long as he was going to maintain a job off the farm and get part of his income from that source, then this appeared to me to be detrimental to the establishment of an economic farm unit. I think this has been wrong. Many of the people in my area are working in mines as a means to supplement their income from the farms. Their wives and families operate uneconomic farm units, and the farmers themselves look upon employment in the mines as a temporary measure to enable them to get enough ready cash to provide the

Farm Credit Act
machinery that will make their farms economic and provide them with a fairly decent standard of living.
The inclusion of other types of income such as this has always been considered in northern Ontario to be an adjunct to farm operations. For many years farmers in the Ottawa valley and the upper Ottawa have used their farm horses in the bush camps during periods of the year when they have little work to do on the farms, and they have done this in order to supplement their farm incomes. However, by doing so it has made it much more difficult for them to establish that they are farmers with economic farm units.
Much credit is due to the minister for introducing these changes. They will be of great value and I see a relationship between them and the efforts being made to help industrial workers faced with the problems of automation. They are provided with retraining programs to enable them to take advantage of new employment, and during their attendance on training programs they have been assisted by payments to themselves and their families. There is a great similarity to that in the redirecting of farmers who will now be able to obtain enough money from the corporation to maintain the operation of their farms during their transition period from, for example, dairy farming to beef production. However the wishes and requirements of individual farmers should be borne in mind, together with the basic agricultural characteristics of the areas in which they live. If these two things are kept in mind I am sure this change will be an advantageous one, not only for the individual who will be placed on an economic farm unit but also for the establishment of a more sound and reasonable form of agriculture.
It is generally conceded that one of the great problems is the inability of a farmer to make a major change in his production schedule. If a man is in dairy cattle and wishes to change to beef cattle then he will go through a period of approximately two years in which no income will flow from his beef production. However if we can allow him enough money to maintain his family and operate his farm during that period, then we will have come a long way toward allowing him to make a change from a non-economic farm operation to one which will be economic.
In any change that is made in the direction of the agricultural economy we should bear in mind that there is a great need for education of the farmer. After reading the statements made by various officials in the province of Ontario, in the 10 counties that were described as being considered for this type of

change-over from dairy to beef production, we have to consider how we are to provide the education that will be necessary in order to make that change.
It has been said by some of the agricultural representatives of the provincial departments of agriculture that this education can only be provided for young people, but I suggest that the change-over can take place much more rapidly, and be more acceptable to the young people in their adult years, if education is supplied similar to that which is supplied to the factory worker who is undergoing a similar transition from one type of employment to another. We should consider the possibility of providing some type of agricultural extension courses for adults which would allow them to have the benefit of instruction given by credit corporation officials and by officials of the various agricultural colleges throughout the country. Such courses could be arranged in the wintertime, and aid for them could be provided by the federal government. I believe this would help make possible the transition we all want, the transition that would result in a more uniform, more productive and much more acceptable agricultural economy.
We should also consider the possibility of providing agricultural training in secondary schools which would help fit our young rural people to accept the advantages that can come to them following on an understanding of the economics of agriculture and the problems facing it. This is a serious problem, because many farmers have consistently resisted change in any form at all, whether it be in credit, in direction, or in the type of farm they are operating. They have resisted change mainly because they are unable to see any advantage in it for themselves and their families, or for the way of life to which they are dedicated.
There are some who will say that this type of education cannot be provided, but I am sure they are the same people who said a few years ago that it would be impossible to provide it in the field of labour. One has only to look at the assistance given by unemployment insurance and the Department of Labour to see the advantages coming from that type of education.
I believe these changes are very radical, in fact sufficiently radical for the minister to refer them to the agricultural committee. These are new ideas and the minister has nothing to be ashamed of in advancing them. On the contrary he has much to take credit for, and it is essential that the country and hon. members of this house know the advantages and know exactly what the minister is trying to do.

When we discuss agriculture in this house we have a tendency-and I am no exception- to cover the whole waterfront. While this may not be quite in keeping with the rules, while it may not have the relevancy it appears to have, there is nothing more complicating to the solution of agricultural problems. For that reason I hope the minister will refer the bill to the committee where the agricultural organizations of the country will have the advantage of discussing the legislation, making recommendations, and being fully informed of its advantageous effects. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, by sending it to a committee I am confident that both that procedure and the legislation itself would go a long way toward helping solve the problems facing agriculture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is really the first opportunity I have had to congratulate you on your election to the distinguished office of Speaker. Within the short time you have held the chair you have shown good judgment, impartiality and patience. I should like also to express the same sentiments in regard to the Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees. The debate so far on this bill has been very interesting. I think very many good ideas have come from all sides of the house. I wish only to review our farm credit facilities during the past 32 years in order that we may see how far we have progressed in this regard, so that some hon. members may be less prone to criticize so severely what we have before us today.
The Canadian farm loans act of 1929, although limited in its scope, its operation hobbled by the restrictive policy of the previous administration, nevertheless has served a useful purpose. Its record was not too impressive. Long before this administration took office there was a general feeling in the agricultural industry that a new farm credit program was necessary for the survival of the Canadian family farm. It was felt that experienced farmers who were raised on the soil, who loved their soil, should be given a chance to stay on it and preserve the traditions of the family farm. It was apparent that this was impossible within the scope of the Canadian farm loans act of 1929.
As usual, representations were made by farm leaders and farm organizations to our predecessors in government. Briefs were presented pleading for a more generous set-up. But, as usual, these representations and briefs were swept under the carpet and nothing was done. True, a few minor amendments to the farm loans act were passed in 1956 and 1957 with the intention of improving credit facilities, but the tight money policy of the
Farm Credit Act
previous administration did not give the industry the services it deserved or to which it was entitled.
This government took office in 1957. It followed a policy of consulting those who were most greatly concerned, and it set up an interdepartmental committee which took into its confidence prominent individual farmers and farm organizations. These people were pleased with the change of policy and co-operated wholeheartedly. They were glad to give their views and were pleased to see that the government did not take a know-it-all attitude, from which they had suffered under the previous administration. The outcome of these consultations was an agreement by all concerned that there would have to be a new farm credit policy with certain basic principles within which the new legislation would function. These basic principles had to be embodied in the new legislation, and I think the Minister of Agriculture has stated the results in considerable detail. But the most striking was that special consideration had to be given to capital requirements of acceptable and experienced young men who wished to establish themselves on the farm. This was probably the most revolutionary idea.
For comparison purposes as between the farm loans of 1929 and the Farm Credit Act that followed it, I should make some reference to what the farm loans act of 1929 provided before I proceed with this analysis. I shall refer to the provisions of the present Farm Credit Act to show that the criticisms we have heard from the opposition benches about this loan policy being discriminatory are best levelled at the previous legislation and at those who administered it before this government came into power. The old act was under the administration of the minister of finance and provided loans on first mortgages on farm lands, with amounts not exceeding 50 per cent of the actual value of the farm lands. Buildings were only considered to the extent that they added to the value of the farm unit. The term of repayment was 25 years, which was amended in 1956. There were no amendments between 1929 and 1956; the legislation was practically dormant. But in 1956 the term of repayment was amended to 30 years. This service, although available throughout the years, as I have already mentioned, had a very unimpressive record up to the year 1957 when the Conservative government took office. Throughout the years this legislation was on the books no serious effort was made by the then administration to expand or improve lending facilities or to encourage farmers to avail themselves of the opportunities this service offered. Barring an insignificant

Farm Credit Act
amendment in 1956 which, as I have already-mentioned, extended the term of repayment to 30 years, raised the maximum amount of the loan to $15,000 based on 65 per cent of the actual value of the land, nothing whatever was done.
In 1957 when the Conservative government took office it changed the tight money policy of its predecessors. It tried, with some success, to expand the facilities of the loan board, and the record tabled by the Minister of Agriculture and found on page 591 of Hansard speaks for itself. In the year 195758 the number of borrowers increased almost twofold, and loans increased to well over $19 million. In the following year, 1958-59, of course, a part of 1959 was under the new legislation. The number of borrowers increased, the amount lent was well over $28 million. I ask the house to compare that with the $3 million lent annually under the previous administration. A new credit plan was in the making. It resulted in the introduction into the house of the Farm Credit Act in 1959 and the repeal of the farm loans act after it had been on the books for a period of 30 years.
Time does not permit me, Mr. Speaker, to quote doubts, misgivings and severe criticism heaped upon this legislation by the opposition when this new act was introduced. I refer, of course, to the introduction of the Farm Credit Act. But it has proved to be a blessing to the industry. If proof of the pudding is in the eating, then in a few short years the loans have increased both in number and size. I would again refer the house to the table put into Hansard by the Minister of Agriculture. For the fiscal 1960-61 the number of borrowers increased to well over
5,000	and the amount lent to over $52 million. In the fiscal year 1961-62 the number of borrowers increased to over 6,000, and the aggregate amount lent to well over $68 million.
I submit, sir, that the estimate by the minister that the 1962-63 loans under this legislation will be well over $80 million is very conservative and will be easily achieved. The new credit policy differs from the old as night differs from day, because it provides for two types of mortgage loans.
In part II, a standard mortgage loan can be made up to $20,000 or 75 per cent of the value of the farm lands given in security, whichever is the lesser, to be secured by a first mortgage on the lands with interest at 5 per cent actually spelled out in the act and repayable in a term of 30 years on an amortised basis. Life insurance on a group basis is made available by the corporation at the option
[Mr. Mandziuk.3
of the borrower in an amount equal to the normal outstanding amount of the loan.
In part HI of the act, a revolutionary step was taken in a package deal mortgage loan designed for capable and experienced young farmers between the ages of 21 and 45 years starting out with limited capital resources. The limit on this loan is $27,500 or 75 per cent of the value of the farmlands, whichever is the lesser, and a chattel mortgage on livestock and farm equipment was accepted as a collateral security for the loan.
The corporation was required to supervise the borrower's farm operation until the loan was reduced to a certain figure, and experienced officials are always ready and willing to help young farmers and guide them in their first years on the farm. This type of loan has been very popular in Manitoba and I am sure that in time these borrowers will establish prosperous farms.
There were some criticisms directed at the insistence of the corporation that in order to qualify for loans, farms should form economic units. Let us bear in mind that these loans are not grants, or a form of relief to farmers. They are intended to assist farmers to make their concerns economic units. An economic unit is a farm which enables its operator to earn each year a decent living for himself and for his family, to pay the operating costs, and, third, to provide for retirement of the loan. The aim here is to establish an economic unit. The amount of the loan is fairly large, but the borrower is compelled to carry life insurance provided by the corporation.
These loans have kept many farmers on the land when otherwise they would have drifted to the cities because of lack of capital with which to start farms. Borrowers have taken advantage of these facilities and there is every indication that they are a success.
During the resolution stage some opposition speakers were severely critical, and they spearheaded their attacks by saying there had been discrimination against the small farm. This does not appear to be true. I have not had a single complaint in my constituency against the corporation on the ground that the size of a farm was the reason for the refusal of a loan. However, we did not hear from opposition critics any definition of what constitutes a small farm, or a large farm, and this is understandable because no definition is possible. The effective size of the farm does not depend entirely upon its area in acres, and even in this latter respect standards differ from province to province. For example, a large farm in my constituency would be considered a small farm in Saskatchewan or Alberta, while a small farm in my constituency would be considered a large

farm in some of the eastern provinces. The average size of the loans has increased, but that is no indication that loans have been withheld from small farmers. If hon. members glance at the table put on record in Hansard at page 591 by the Minister of Agriculture they will see that the number of borrowers has doubled and, in some cases, tripled and that the average amount of the loan is around $11,000. So there certainly must have been smaller loans. This rise in the amount of the average loan seems to shock some members of the opposition and, in particular, the hon. member for Assiniboia. That is understandable, because the Liberals while they were in power held down the size of the loans, hobbling the farm loan board to such an extent that in some years the amount lent to farmers was less than $2 million. They suppressed the desire of farmers to expand their holdings and never gave them enough to enable them to take advantage of the opportunities which existed. This is not the case with the present government.
We have to admit that the family farm, out west at least, is becoming larger in area. The horse days are over and these faithful animals have been replaced by mechanized farm equipment. This is expensive and the farm unit must become larger to enable the farmer to pay for its cost. In other words, it must be set to work to pay for itself.
Another criticism that we heard from the opposition was that the eastern farmer was not getting benefits of this loan policy to the same extent as the western farmer, and the blame for this situation is tagged on to the Minister of Agriculture and on the corporation. This, in my opinion, is unjustified and without foundation. Such criticism could best be levelled against the previous administration which, for almost 30 years, administered the act. I should like to know what they have done to boast about which entitles them to talk about unfairness in the service to the eastern provinces. As a proof that this charge is groundless, may I refer this house to the schedules put in Hansard by the Minister of Agriculture and appearing on page 595 under the heading "Statement by Provinces of Farm Loans approved during Fiscal Years." All hon. members need to look at are the figures for the province of Quebec. They will see that in the nine months of the present year to the end of September, 262 loans have been processed to a total of almost $4 million compared to 109 loans amounting to $1,750,000 in the fiscal year 1961-1962. Does this not show that the eastern farmer is realizing that these facilities are always ready and available to him and that all he has to do is to act? One can hardly expect the Minister of Agriculture
Farm Credit Act
to go around from place to place asking farmers to take loans. That has not been done in the west; every farmer knows these facilities are available.
I am glad to see that one of the amendments provides the corporation with additional lending capital, and I am sure these facilities will be welcomed by the agricultural industry. I am really pleased by the amendments which have been put forward. I believe they will expand the facilities which are now available and, in particular, that they will provide greater opportunities for the smaller farmer. As I have said, the size of a farm in itself is not an indication of its economic importance. I am glad to note that greater weight is to be placed on the value of equipment for specialized projects-greenhouses, for example and the special buildings required to raise poultry or hogs. Farmers engaged in such operations are not expected to hold large acreages. They will be able to take advantage of the lending provisions by reason of this proposed amendment. I was also happy to see that the amendments which are proposed will permit the making of loans to farmers on the basis of secondary incomes. Until now, the corporation took into consideration only income deriving directly from the farm, as a gauge of the ability of a farmer to repay. At the present time, any secondary income which a farmer may possess is taken into consideration, and his chances of qualifying for a loan are improved.
As I said at the outset, I was very pleased with the many good ideas, good addresses and flattering remarks about this legislation. I was to a certain extent surprised at the lambasting that the hon. member for Assiniboia gave this bill. It was a repeat performance, practically verbatim, of what he said on the resolution stage. He called this bill a farce. He said it was not far-reaching enough and was too technical. I wish to draw to his attention that it is not so technical that the Western Producer in the news item to which I referred was able to analyse the bill very carefully, and to say that more farmers stand a chance of loans. The hon. member also said it does not give the small farmer a chance. The only authority he relies upon is that of himself. He bemoans the fact that 55 per cent of those applying for loans did not get them; but he does not say that he would just open the door without regard to the farmer's credit, or without regard to the farmer's operation, or without regard to whether it is an economic unit and will give him a reasonable standard of living, pay his living expenses, and the opportunity to pay the loan back. That is the only measure which a business corporation can use.

Farm Credit Act
This is public money which is involved. The Farm Credit Corporation is one which is not intended to make money, but on the other hand it is not intended that the public treasury should replenish its funds because of maladministration, careless financing, or carelessness through making laws. All in all, I would suggest that the hon. member for Assiniboia take a few tips from the hon. member for Leeds. He was more reasonable. The only point with which I would agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia is in his complaint against the $50 charged as an inspection fee. I personally think that that is high. The minister has promised that the regulations will be revised, and I hope this fee will be reduced. I would not do away with it altogether. I like the suggestion which was made by the hon. member for Leeds, who said that it could be levied by way of a graduated scale, because to some of these farmers who apply for small loans, $50 really is a deterrent.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that I have not taken up too much time, but I wanted to give a review of our farm lending facilities over the last 32 years or so and to show this house that we have made progress. There is always room for improvement. I know that the minister does not feel that this legislation is perfect, but it is as near perfect as it is possible to make it at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the resolution stage of this legislation some weeks ago the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) gave a comprehensive outline of the Liberal party's farm policy, which was ably supported by several members on this side of the house. This afternoon the hon. member, in his speech on second reading of this bill, made some very worthwhile suggestions, not the least of which was that this bill should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture so that the committee might be able to summon before it expert advice from those organizations which are directly concerned with the welfare of agriculture in this country. Therefore, I shall confine myself to one or two aspects of the problem encountered by comparatively small farmers operating in districts such as northwestern Ontario.
To begin with, the effect of the amendments to the Farm Credit Act is to provide a greater range of financial assistance to the small farmers, and if it is to be of any assistance to those in greater need, then I suggest that the farmers of northwestern Ontario should share in the benefits of this legislation. A change in the regulations governing the appraisal of small farm holdings,

such as small dairy farms, greenhouse operators, poultrymen, woodlot farmers and others, whose operations require relatively high investment in buildings on small areas of land, will be an incentive to the get-back-to-the-farm movement, if this financial assistance could be provided, which could attract many from the ranks of the unemployed.
This bill is designed to meet the needs of Canadian farmers with long term farm mortgage credit, the operations of which are under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture. It provides an increase in the lending capacity of the corporation by $100 million. That is, of course, welcomed by all concerned. The Farm Credit Act was enacted in 1959 and succeeded the old Canadian farm loan board. The difference, my friends, which distinguishes the new from the old is that the Farm Credit Corporation, in addition to the five members of the board, has an advisory committee composed of 11 men representing all the provinces with the exception of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. It can readily be seen that the adviser who assesses the farmer's application is indeed the most important person in the organization. He is the one who interviews the applicant and decides whether or not the loan is in the farmer's best interests, or whether in his opinion the farmer can expect a sufficient income to pay operating costs, provide himself and his family with a reasonably good living, and permit repayment of the loan.
The latest available report of the corporation for the year ending March, 1961 contains the following outline of the duties of the farm credit adviser.
It is also a duty and responsibility of the farm credit adviser to make known to his farming community the services and benefits available under the Farm Credit Act, and to promote the use of these services where they will further the object of the legislation.
To fulfil all of these essential functions and to earn and retain the confidence and good will of the farming community requires not only technical competence but integrity, fairness, good judgment, a keen sense of responsibility and devotion to duty. It must therefore continue to be corporation policy to maintain exacting standards in the selection and training of its farm credit advisers, since the success or failure of the legislation is very much in their hands.
By and large this corporation has filled a great need and has also made a creditable contribution to the development of agriculture in certain areas of the country, notably in the prairie provinces. Unfortunately, however, it has not been of the assistance expected in areas where, for the most part, farms are of the small dairy type, with mixed crops and woodlots, such as those which are in the majority of cases found in northwestern

Ontario. The result has been that not many farmers in my constituency have been able to obtain loans under the act.
The principal reason for this neglect is that the nearest credit adviser is located in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and the Ontario member is located in the vicinity of Toronto. This is a definite handicap, as northwestern Ontario is a very large territory, and farm conditions there are vastly different from those confronting the wheat farmers of the west and the opulent land squires of southeastern Ontario. The result is that while these men are charged with the responsibility to make known to the farming community the services and benefits available under the Farm Credit Act and to promote the use of these services, their assessment of the merits of an application is invariably downgraded.
I wish to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the size of the fluid milk market and the quality of the farms involved deserve greater consideration on the part of the corporation.
Encouragement should be given to the development of beef enterprises. This is a field which could very easily transform the meagre resources of the farmers of the Thunder Bay area into an industry of national importance. The soil is particularly good for potato growing. Moreover, district farmers on several occasions have won honours at agricultural shows in Toronto and in other cities.
The figure for approval of farm loans in the lakehead area is approximately 20 per cent of all applications, while in the rest of the province of Ontario the figure is about 50 per cent. Manitoba enjoyed the approval of nearly 70 per cent of all applications, a circumstance which leads me to believe that there must be something wrong with the appraisal of the agricultural potential of northwestern Ontario.
I also submit that those charged with the responsibility of administering the act should consider the appointment of an adviser from the lakehead area who would have an understanding of local land values and be fully conversant with the market possibilities of the district which, in the opinion of many of our pioneers and experts in the assessment of soil, has plenty of productive acreage with which to supply its own needs and to have a sizeable amount for export.
I have already indicated that the district offers excellent opportunities for the expansion of production of dairy products. A few years ago a thriving cheese factory was operating in the village of Stanley, some 12 miles from the city of Fort William. Unfortunately, however, the promoters were forced to close down the operation because they lacked sufficient capital with which to expand. At present some people are interested in 27507-3-77
Farm Credit Act
starting a modern cheese making establishment, using European processing methods. If the participants in this enterprise should require capital I hope the Farm Credit Corporation will not be stingy in approving an adequate loan.
In areas where the establishment of a woodlot operation is more suitable, the Farm Credit Corporation should not hesitate to give assistance to worthy applicants even though their collateral may not be in line with their needs.
The ever growing needs of farmers for capital and credit for farm operation and for contented family living in all parts of Canada require a wider acceptance of responsibility by the government in recognizing that the general health and growth of the Canadian economy is linked up with the workers of the soil and that therefore it should be good business to encourage a high level of production and capital investment.
The submission of the national farmers union made to the government on February 15, 1961, rejected the widely held opinion that technology and efficiency demand the removal of the majority of farm families from the land. The brief went on to use these words:
We do not subscribe to the theory that the activities and institutions of men are determined solely by technology and economics regardless of human and social values, but hold that technological developments can and must he adjusted to serve the human, social and economic needs of men.
We believe that the family farm is the most efficient unit in terms not only of production, but also in terms of soil conservation and human and social values. We therefore believe that the preservation of the family farm is of importance to farm families as well as to the nation as a whole.
I for one certainly subscribe to these sentiments, which are opposed to the farm people of Canada becoming workers in a factory in the field instead of workers on a happy family farm. Canada's best interest will be served in the end by a large number of mixed farms rather than by a few large, specialized farm units.
According to the 1961 census, the farm population of the district of Thunder Bay in northwestern Ontario has decreased since 1956 from 1,486 to 850, a decline of 46 per cent; and in the same five year period the cultivated area has shrunk from 33,993 acres to 25,614 acres. This is an alarming situation. I hope these amendments will help to attract more people to the land and will make those now on the land more contented and prosperous.
The statement of the minister that this government will settle for nothing less than adequate assistance to the farmers is good news, provided it is meant to help all the

Farm Credit Act
farmers in need of a loan to consolidate and to develop their holdings, however small their cultivated area may be. The establishing of a policy by which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would provide loans for housing on farms, without the requirement that the farmer mortgage his land, one which would prevent the obtaining of credit for other needs, should be given favourable consideration.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the success of the legislation before the house will be measured-and I wish to point this out specifically to the minister-not by the intent but by the number of loans made to those in need of assistance whose collateral or holdings may not meet the strict requirements, the observance of which has characterized the methods of approval under which the corporation has operated in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate you on being elected Speaker of this House of Commons. Coming as I do from Alberta, I know you will perform your duties with dignity and wisdom. However, I should like to say that this Farm Credit Corporation has worked very well since its introduction three years ago. A great deal of credit goes to the Minister of Agriculture, and also in the last couple of years to T. H. Rutherford who has just retired from work and who, I am sure all will agree, put a great deal of work into this corporation.
I should also like to say a word about the way this measure has worked in Alberta. It has worked very well and we have had a very capable superintendent in Alberta by the name of Mr. George O'Brien. He has put a lot of work into the administration of this act. I do agree, to a certain extent, that the $50 appraisal fee is rather high. I should like to see an amendment introduced by means of which we would have a $20 appraisal fee which would be gradually raised according to the size of the loan obtained. Reference was made to the fact that in one constituency several people had forefeited this $50 fee. This is not the case in Alberta. The farm is appraised and if the loan is not granted the $50 fee is not required.
Since this Farm Credit Corporation has worked so well I cannot, for the life of me, understand why we are getting so much criticism from the Liberal party in the last
[Mr. Badanai.l
few days. It seems to me that they are embarrassed when a comparison is made with the legislation that they adopted in former years. It is interesting to note that this criticism is coming from the new members who have come into the house during this session, or those who have joined the Liberal party from other ranks. It is interesting to go back to the 1959 Hansard at a time when this Farm Credit Corporation was under consideration. I should like to read to you some of the words spoken by the hon. member for Assini-boia at that time I quote from page 5933:
The corporation set up under this measure will replace the Canadian farm loan board.
Now, the Canadian farm loan board was introduced by the Liberal party.
Over the years I have bitterly complained about the narrow concept of the board in processing applications.
He was complaining then and he is complaining now.
I have been pleased to observe that in recent years some improvement was made in its administration and a larger number of loans have been made under the act. I have, however, a substantial file of letters from people whose applications for loans have been turned down by the board. I think that in substantial measure the criticism made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture before the banking and commerce committee in 1956 is still valid, that this board has taken a conservative attitude in the processing of applications.
I would like the minister to tell me when he replies if in actual practice the board has denied large areas of western Canada loans under this act. I also want to know if the new corporation will have a more efficient system of filing than the board apparently had. I have received letters from people in my constituency complaining that their application for loans were turned down although they felt their financial position would encourage the board to grant them a loan. I have suspected that large areas of western Canada have been declared areas where the board will not grant loans.
This was his criticism of the Liberal government when he sat as a C.C.F. member. Today he is criticizing again. I agree with the statement of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) when he said that the hon. member for Assiniboia just likes to hear himself talk.
Then, we have the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh). He said in the house a while ago that in his district, under the old board, many more farmers were granted loans than under the present set-up. Then, he went on to preach us a little sermon, and then he disappeared. I am glad that he is here tonight and that I may be able to put him back on the right track with a little information. Later, we had the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), who was around here before supper, and he came up with another statement to the effect that the westerner was getting more money from this corporation

than the easterner. These are a few of the things we have heard within the last few days.
Just let us look at the record in order to be fair about the situation. In Ontario during 1960-61 there was $19,151,700 lent to farmers, the highest for any province in Canada. Then, these people in Ontario say they are not getting their share. We hear these people from the Liberal party talking about a board that is not working well. What happened? Well, in 1952-53, under the old board there were 1,685 loans granted for a total amount of $5,852,300. During 1960-61 the credit corporation that this government introduced granted 5,597 loans for a total amount of $60,704,050. What a difference over the last few years. Then, we are criticized. I do not know what they want. They seem to be embarrassed. Let us keep politics out of good legislation like this. They are trying to get this measure sent to a committee in order to hold it up. This is good legislation; let us put it before the people who can make use of it.
I should like to say a word to those members who spoke from that corner of the house with reference to the problems of Quebec. I sympathize with them because they have problems in that part of the country. My parents came from New Brunswick. A couple of years ago I travelled through that part of Quebec and northern New Brunswick. I saw these people, and they have problems. They have a few acres, and they are trying to make a living from them. I recall that my father used to talk about taking a team to haul logs all winter and living off salt pork. They will not be able to do that today. We will try to meet these problems with the amendments we have introduced. Let us get on with this good work and not play politics here, in the house.

-no loan shall be made to any person under the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act on or after the day on which this act comes into force.
So, in effect, a Conservative government made long term mortgage loans available for fishermen, and the Liberal government took them away. Now the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate wants them re-introduced and one can only suggest that since he was in the cabinet in 1955 there must have been a split between the then minister of finance, Mr. Harris, and himself, and one can only assume that he lost the battle.

I am very sorry, but apparently my office forgot to remind those hon. members that a representative was appointed in Port Arthur in February, 1962, and since that time he has processed 29 loans in the area he services.

Farm Credit Act
loans totalling $141,800; in the Kenora district, 3 loans totalling $20,500; in the Rainy river district, 17 loans totalling $167,000, making a total of 59 loans and a lump sum of $621,900.
I think this point makes it clear that in examination of the work of the Farm Credit Corporation I have been frank with the house in bringing out the good points which that legislation has accomplished and showing how there has been a tremendous increase in the loans granted over the last three years. In fact there were more granted in the last three years than were granted by all governments in the previous 30 years.
The amendments before us are designed to broaden the basis for loans and make the terms more flexible so that good work can be done in all districts of Canada. In saying that I am not only including British Columbia, parts of the prairies, northwestern Ontario, and the eastern parts of Ontario but also Quebec and the maritimes where, with this new type of broadened legislation, we can do a better job.
I do not need to tell the house that the Farm Credit Corporation does its most useful work during the winter months when the officials have time to talk with the farmers and discuss their programs for the next year. This is why I am anxious to have this legislation passed as soon as possible, and this is the reason why the government introduced it as the second piece of legislation since parliament assembled. We are now hopeful that the legislation will be passed quickly so that we can then take under advisement the backlog of applications for loans which were not successful because they had not met certain criteria under the act as it existed up to now.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I thank the hon. member opposite for his help. The question I should like to have the minister explain to me is why we want to increase the number of loans and the amount of money to be lent principally to the farmers of eastern

Canada-Quebec and further east-where the number of loans, as has already been mentioned often enough, is very low, and yet at the same time the minister is publicly stating that farmers must decrease their production. I am unable to see in this day and age how you can make a small farm into an economic unit without increasing production. Does this mean that we are going to refuse loans to the small dairy farmer who wants to turn his farm into an economic unit? I think I am right in saying that this warning was given to the dairy farmers of Quebec and Ontario; at least, according to the newspaper report it was. There is probably some very simple explanation for this, but I should like to hear it from the minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad you used the word "paradox" to describe this intervention in the debate by an hon. member from probably the most solidly urban riding in Canada. I can give him a very short answer, Mr. Chairman, and that is that he consult Mr. Lemoyne, who knows something about this matter of stabilization of prices and support prices. He also knows something about farm credit. If the hon. member does not know who Mr. Lemoyne is, he ran as Liberal candidate for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot but did not make out very well because our party whip looked after him too well. He went on public record in the last few days as coming out and supporting the leadership which I am giving to the small farmer, and my efforts to give him justice. I would advise the hon. member, in the interest of his own political future, to go to people who know something about it, and they can explain it to him.
The hon. member has asked me one question concerning the extension of the amount of money which is being lent, and that is a serious question which I shall try to answer. The answer is very simple. Farming today needs credit. But in any modern business, and that includes farming, you do not continue pressuring farmers into a type of operation yielding a product of which there is a surplus and the future of which is not bright. You try, in discussing the possibilities for the future with them, to direct them to where returns are higher. That is why I say that there is no paradox. The farmers need more money to enable them to get at things which are possible, and into things where they can make money. If any farmer comes in and asks for money for a dairy operation, and he has a plan which will meet the criteria of the act, then he will get a loan. The Farm Credit Corporation have no right to decide what the farmer is to do. It is a free enterprise society. But as I mentioned in opening the debate today, we do put down all the alternative uses which we see for his land, and we put down the value of the returns under each type

of operation and let him choose. However, at the present time, with present cattle prices and the floor price of cattle being what it is, and the future market for cattle being so well assured, if he can see more money, a surer income and a higher return for many years and shifts to beef cattle, we think that is in the interests of the country. But he makes the choice.
So, Mr. Chairman, there is no paradox at all. Farming today is in desperate need of capital, but not capital to spend on things you do not need. The hour is late and I do not want to go into a long description of this matter. I can put it in one sentence. Fifty years ago we used to spend much of our time and a great deal of our acreage growing brome grass to feed horses. There is no use growing brome grass today because we use tractors. The same applies to any section of the farming industry. We put the money into where the need is.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question. There seems to be the impression that we have a $50 appraisal fee charged for all types of loans to farmers, whether they are made by the Farm Credit Corporation or under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The Farm Credit Corporation has money for larger loans, and the Farm Improvement Loans Act provides for smaller loans. Is there any appraisal fee charged to an applicant under the Farm Improvement Loans Act?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
As I understand the question, the hon. member is asking whether appraisal fees are applied on all types of loans? The answer is no. An appraisal fee is applied only on loans which are made on long term mortgage under the Farm Credit Act, through the Farm Credit Corporation. Out of the ones who do apply for the long term credit loan-and the turn-downs are roughly one half, 55 per cent-very few of the 55 per cent, I hazard the guess almost none, pay the $50. There is another type of credit, an intermediate type of credit, where you walk into a bank without any appraisal fee or any charge at all for a lawyer. You put down your request for the loan, sign the paper, and get the money without any cost to you, and the interest rate is the same. For the great majority of loans there is no appraisal fee whatsoever. It is only with loans which are substantial and where we have to do a lot of work. I have already told the committee that we have under advisement a new type of appraisal fee; but I will not say
Farm Credit Act
anything about that until the corporation announces or tells me what they are going to recommend we do about it.

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I do not think the Farm Credit Corporation has gone into that small type of loan since 1959.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: I am sorry; I meant the Canadian farm loan board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY

The farm loan board were supposed to deal with long term credit and to give fairly large loans. They gave a moderate type of loan which had ceilings of $4,000, $9,000 and $15,000 at various times. Therefore their loans were smaller. As I understand it, their policy was to clamp down and give as few loans as possible. There is no connection at all between the two. You might describe the farm loan board as a small loans operation. They did not have a very large ceiling.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: The parliamentary secretary says that he gets it under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Who brought in the Farm Improvement Loans Act? speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I mentioned once before, Mr. Speaker, we are in the hands of the house. We had hoped earlier this week to have completed general debate when we were iii committee of ways and means. That is something that did not happen. However, there has been considerable consultation today. Our proposal now is that we go back into committee of ways and means tomorrow, which is Friday. Then if the house completes the general discussion in committee of ways and means and is prepared by five o'clock to restrict discussion to the first resolution, or to the other resolutions if we reach them, then we will proceed with a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday. Otherwise, if the house finds it cannot complete the general discussion on the ways and means resolution tomorrow, it seems to me we would have to go into ways and means on Monday and

Tuesday. However, if we make that headway which I suggest, we would have a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday. What would follow during the balance of the week I am not prepared to say at the moment. However, we would perhaps endeavour to complete any unfinished resolutions in ways and means.

Perhaps the minister would permit me to make one observation, and it
Business of the House
is this: So far as my friends are concerned, I think I can assure him we are prepared to co-operate with the government in any endeavour to complete the general debate in committee of ways and means by five o'clock at the latest.
